setupSteps: Warm up first. 1 to 3 minutes of gentle cat-cow or knee hugs (Yoga & Stretch 10) and a few pelvic tilts on the back.
Floor. Flat, non-slip mat or a rug on a dry floor. Avoid slippery tiles for the feet.
Lie down. On your back, arms alongside the body, palms down.

Knees and feet. Bend the knees. Feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart (about two fists apart, est.), parallel, toes pointing straight ahead. Walk the heels in until your fingertips can just touch the back of the heels (a common teaching test).

Neck. Keep the back of the head on the floor and the chin neutral (not tucked hard onto the chest). Look at the ceiling for the whole hold. If the neck feels strained, slide a thin folded towel under the shoulders (not under the head).

Block (optional, supported version). Keep a block, firm cushion or folded blanket stack within reach. Use the lowest height first (a lower block is more stable; sources note the tallest height is the least stable).
Clothing. Stretchy pants; no tight jeans; fitted top so the camera sees the shoulders and hips.
Camera. Phone on the floor or a low stool, 2 to 2.5 m to the side, hip height or lower, so the whole body from shoulders to feet is in frame (see sections 11 and 12).

steps.title: Lie down and relax
steps.action: lie on your back, arms by the sides, palms down, knees bent.
steps.feel: the whole back heavy on the floor.

steps.title: Set the feet
steps.action: feet flat, hip-width apart, parallel, heels close to the buttocks.
steps.feel: the whole sole of each foot pressing down, weight even.

steps.title: Tilt the pelvis a little
steps.action: press the lower back softly toward the floor, then release; stay in a neutral low back.
steps.feel: the lower belly gently switching on.

steps.title: Press the feet and arms down
steps.action: push the feet into the floor and the backs of the arms and palms into the mat.
steps.feel: thighs and buttocks waking up; shoulders firm.

steps.title: Lift the hips
steps.action: on the in-breath, raise the tailbone first, then the lower back, then the middle back, as one smooth movement, until the thighs are about level with the floor (parallel to each other and to the floor).
steps.feel: the buttocks and back of the thighs working; a light stretch at the front of the hips.

steps.title: Keep the neck still
steps.action: keep the gaze on the ceiling. Do not turn the head left or right; do not lift the chin.
steps.feel: the back of the neck long and free; weight on the shoulders and upper arms, not the neck.

steps.title: Check the knees and thighs
steps.action: keep the knees over the ankles and the thighs parallel (not splayed). If the knees drift out, press the outer edges of the feet down; a block or strap between the thighs can help.

steps.title: Optional: slide the block under the sacrum
steps.action: lower the hips slightly, slide a block (lowest height first) under the sacrum (the flat bone at the base of the spine, not the lower back), then rest the weight on it. Let the feet press lightly; the legs can soften.
steps.feel: supported; the back of the pelvis resting; no pinching in the lower back.

steps.title: Hold
steps.action: stay with an even, slow nose breath. Unsupported: about 5 breaths (about 25 seconds, est.); sources range from 10 to 30 seconds (AYUSH-style source) up to 30 to 60 seconds (5 to 10 breaths). Supported on a block: 1 to 3 minutes for a beginner (est.; sources say 2 to 5 minutes).
steps.feel: steady effort in the buttocks and thighs, no pain, no neck pressure.
steps.breathing: slow nose breaths, count each out-breath.

steps.title: Lower slowly
steps.action: on an out-breath, lower the spine one part at a time: upper back first, then the middle back, then the lower back, and the tailbone last. If a block is under you, lift the hips slightly first and slide it out, then lower.
steps.feel: each vertebra touching the floor in order.

steps.title: Rest
steps.action: let the knees fall together or hug the knees to the chest.
steps.feel: the lower back soft and released.
steps.visualCheck: back flat on the floor; neck free.

commonMistakes.title: Turning or lifting the head
commonMistakes.text: Turning or lifting the head. It strains the neck, the most common cause of bridge-related neck pain. Fix: keep the gaze on the ceiling and the head still; place a thin towel under the shoulders if the neck feels loaded.

commonMistakes.title: Knees splaying out or falling in
commonMistakes.text: Knees splaying out or falling in. It stresses the knees and takes work off the hips. Fix: keep the feet hip-width and parallel, press the outer edges of the feet down; a block between the thighs can help.

commonMistakes.title: Feet too far from or too close to the buttocks
commonMistakes.text: Feet too far from or too close to the buttocks. Too far strains the hamstrings (cramp); too close pinches the knees. Fix: walk the heels in until the fingertips just brush the heels.

commonMistakes.title: Over-lifting and arching the lower back
commonMistakes.text: Over-lifting and arching the lower back. It compresses the lower back and pushes the ribs up. Fix: lift only until the thighs are level; draw the lower belly in and the tailbone toward the knees.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing the chest up toward the chin
commonMistakes.text: Pushing the chest up toward the chin. It jams the neck (a neck-compression risk named in teaching sources). Fix: let the chest rise only from the lift, not from pulling the chin to it; keep the neck long.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping the hips or letting one hip sag
commonMistakes.text: Dropping the hips or letting one hip sag. Uneven work and a twist in the pelvis. Fix: squeeze the buttocks evenly; lower and reset.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. It raises effort and blood pressure. Fix: slow nose breathing during the whole hold.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping down fast
commonMistakes.text: Dropping down fast. The back and neck get a jolt. Fix: roll down one part at a time, tailbone last.

commonMistakes.title: Block too high or on the lower back
commonMistakes.text: Block too high or on the lower back. It pinches the back and feels unstable. Fix: use the lowest height; place it under the sacrum (flat bone), not the waist.

safetyNotes: Mild effort, never pain. Stop at pain in the neck, back, knee, hip or shoulder.

Neck: keep the head still. A yoga teacher source advises avoiding the pose until a current neck or shoulder injury is healed; a yoga-injury database lists herniated cervical disc among contraindications (snippets). With a neck injury, ask a doctor or an experienced teacher first.
Lower back: do not over-arch. Use a small lift or a block. Stop if pain spreads, or if leg symptoms (tingling, numbness) appear.
Knees: feet close to the hips but not so close the knees pinch; knees over the ankles, no inward collapse.
Digestive: the CYP-style caution lists peptic ulcer and hernia; skip or ask a doctor.

Blood pressure and heart: the CYP-style snippet lists avoiding the practices with cardiac problems or high blood pressure. Bridge is a mild, head-below-hips pose (hips lifted, head on the floor); Harvard Health advises caution about heart-above-head poses in general (snippet). Use short holds, never hold the breath, come out slowly.
Dizziness: after lowering, rest and breathe; sit up slowly.

Stop immediately if you feel: sharp pain in the neck or back, numbness or tingling in the arms or legs, dizziness, chest pain or breathlessness, a cramp in the back of the thigh that does not ease, or a pop or pull.
Spotter: not needed. Gym etiquette: keep the block and mat out of the walkway; do not take the only mat in a crowded stretching area for a long supported hold.

Hold time: 10 to 30 seconds (AYUSH-style), 30 to 60 seconds or 5 to 10 breaths (teaching), several minutes if block-supported. We chose about 5 breaths (about 25 s, est.) unsupported and 1 to 3 minutes supported (est.).
Hand position: hands by the sides, clasped under the back, or holding the ankles. We chose hands by the sides.
Hip height: thighs level in most sources; some push higher. We chose level thighs, not height chasing.
Pregnancy: listed as an avoid pose by some sources, a supported option by others. We chose "ask a doctor; supported only if cleared".

Not found: official CYP text for Setubandhasana (only snippets); an MDNIY technique page; a bridge-specific MET; measured joint-angle norms or EMG for the yoga bridge pose; clinical sources on osteoporosis, postpartum, thyroid, cholesterol for this pose; ACOG wording for this pose; a direct comparison of yoga bridge with glute bridge. Our thresholds are estimates.
